original.target_description: Experiment 1; attitude change toward an alcohol ban among male Princeton undergraduates; a priori orthogonal contrast of high-choice counterattitudinal essay against the two nondissonance conditions (high-choice consonant and low-choice counterattitudinal).

n.exclusions: No Experiment 1 exclusions reported; the participant count and contrast error df of 27 support the full 30-participant analysis.

replication.target_description: Primary classic cognitive-dissonance effect: postessay attitude, high-choice counterattitudinal essay (HC-CE) versus low-choice counterattitudinal essay (LC-CE), aggregated participant data, one-tailed Welch t test. The locator does not specify which of the four primary comparisons on p. 15; this explicitly named classic-effect test is selected.

n.sample_role: Analytic participant counts for postessay attitude in HC-CE and LC-CE, respectively; no summed n computed
n.exclusions: Primary analyses exclude participant-characteristic and session-characteristic cases and one lab over the attrition limit; noncompliant essay writers remain included. Counts are the outcome-specific Table 4 counts, rather than recruited N or the all-condition sample.
n.location: p. 15, Table 4, Primary analyses, Postessay attitude, HC-CE and LC-CE columns; p. 13, Sample size and exclusions

reported_success.quote: we failed to replicate the classic dissonance effect.

notes: Titles verified against the supplied references. Original p.5 is PDF p.5 / printed p.786. Original contrast combines both nondissonance controls; replication selected test compares HC-CE with LC-CE only, using postessay attitude rather than change scores. These are related but different tests, retained separately. Replication p.15 additionally prints attitude-change HC-CE versus LC-CE: t(1,969.56) = 0.38, p = .35, d = 0.017; Table 4 n = 1,060 and 937. Postessay HC-CE versus HC-NE is t(2,408.92) = 6.51, p < .001, d = 0.26; attitude-change HC-CE versus HC-NE is t(1,725.20) = 6.72, p < .001, d = 0.31. Authors report failure of the classic choice-dependent effect while observing a counterattitudinal-versus-neutral essay difference. No metrics converted.
